patient.chief_complaint: Recurrent episodes of suddenly feeling detached from surroundings with an odd smell, followed by confusion and inability to recall the episodes
patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Chen is a 41-year-old right-handed woman and middle school art teacher who was brought to the emergency department by a colleague after a witnessed episode of unresponsiveness at work. Her colleague reports that during a faculty meeting, Ms. Chen suddenly stopped talking mid-sentence, appeared to stare blankly, and then began repetitively picking at her blouse with her left hand while making subtle chewing motions with her mouth. The colleague called her name several times but received no response. The episode lasted approximately 60 to 90 seconds, after which Ms. Chen appeared confused and disoriented for roughly five minutes. She had no memory of the event and was surprised when told what had happened.

Upon further questioning, Ms. Chen reports that over the past eight months she has experienced intermittent episodes of suddenly perceiving an unpleasant, hard-to-describe metallic or burnt smell that she knows is not actually present, followed by a sensation of being disconnected from her surroundings, as though she were watching herself from outside her body. These episodes are brief, lasting 20 to 40 seconds, and she has remained aware during most of them, though occasionally she notices gaps in her memory afterward. She has experienced these episodes approximately two to three times per month and initially attributed them to anxiety or stress at work. She reports that on two occasions in the past three months she woke up in the morning with a bitten tongue and significant muscle soreness, though she has no memory of nocturnal events. She has also noticed increasing difficulty remembering students' names, which she finds unusual and distressing given her previously excellent memory. She denies any recent head trauma, illness, or medication changes. Her migraines have continued at their usual frequency and are phenomenologically different from these new episodes. She has never seen a neurologist for these symptoms and has not had any prior EEG or brain imaging.

eeg.impression: Mildly abnormal EEG. Rare right anterior-mid temporal sharp transients of uncertain significance are noted during drowsiness. These may represent epileptiform activity localizing to the right temporal region, but their morphology overlaps with wicket spikes, a benign variant, and definitive classification is not possible on this limited recording. Additionally, intermittent right temporal polymorphic delta slowing is present, which is nonspecific but may suggest underlying right temporal pathology. No electrographic seizures captured
eeg.limitations: Routine 45-minute recording with significant muscle artifact over temporal channels during portions of wakefulness. No clinical events captured during the study. Prolonged video-EEG monitoring is strongly recommended to resolve the ambiguity of the sharp transients and to capture habitual clinical events.

output.query: temporal lobe epilepsy olfactory aura uncinate seizures lateralization

results.title: Olfactory auras in focal epilepsy: clinical, EEG and MRI correlates
results.summary: Olfactory auras (uncinate fits) are associated with mesial temporal lobe epilepsy. They occur in approximately 5-10% of temporal lobe epilepsy patients and may lateralize to either hemisphere. Unpleasant olfactory hallucinations are more common than pleasant ones.

results.title: Lateralizing value of seizure semiology in temporal lobe epilepsy
results.summary: Contralateral manual automatisms (hand fumbling ipsilateral to seizure onset) and ipsilateral dystonic posturing are reliable lateralizing signs. Olfactory auras alone have limited lateralizing value but combined with other signs improve localization.

results.title: Subtle MRI-negative temporal lobe epilepsy: role of 3T MRI and FDG-PET
results.summary: Approximately 20-30% of temporal lobe epilepsy patients have normal or equivocal 1.5T MRI findings. 3T MRI with epilepsy protocol detects subtle hippocampal sclerosis missed on standard imaging in a significant proportion. FDG-PET adds complementary lateralizing information.

output.proposed: Lamotrigine 25 mg daily, titrate to 200 mg daily over 8 weeks
interactions: Sertraline: No clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction. Both are well tolerated in combination. Sertraline does not significantly affect lamotrigine metabolism.
contraindications: Latex allergy (contact dermatitis) documented -- no cross-reactivity with lamotrigine; heightened vigilance for cutaneous reactions is warranted in patients with any drug or contact allergy history
warnings: Risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis, especially with rapid titration. Must use slow titration schedule.
Any rash during titration should prompt immediate evaluation and consideration of discontinuation
Not teratogenic category D but associated with cleft palate risk at higher doses -- relevant for this woman of childbearing age, counsel on contraception

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Focal epilepsy of right temporal lobe origin with mesial temporal sclerosis (mesial TLE, focal impaired-awareness seizures with olfactory aura)

differential.key_features: Possible if no electrographic correlate captured; ruled out by video-EEG showing ictal pattern coincident with stereotyped semiology.
Olfactory hallucinations can occur in migraine but here the aura is followed by behavioral arrest and amnesia — not migraine.
Hypermotor or nocturnal frontal events absent; oroalimentary automatisms and amnesia favor temporal localization.
TGA episodes are minutes-to-hours of anterograde amnesia without automatisms; semiology here is too brief and stereotyped.
No prodromal lightheadedness, no postural trigger, prolonged post-ictal confusion — inconsistent with syncope.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain detailed seizure history including semiology, aura, automatisms, duration, frequency, witness accounts, and post-ictal features.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Stereotyped focal impaired-awareness events with temporal-lobe aura and post-ictal confusion.
Interictal exam typically normal; subtle memory deficit may be present.

optimal_actions.action: Order EEG (routine first; pursue ambulatory or video-EEG if non-diagnostic) to identify interictal epileptiform discharges and capture habitual events.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Interictal sharps/spikes and/or focal slowing in the anterior temporal region; ictal correlate confirms diagnosis.

optimal_actions.action: Order MRI brain with dedicated epilepsy protocol (thin-cut coronal T1/FLAIR/T2/DWI through the hippocampi).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Hippocampal sclerosis, low-grade tumor (DNET, ganglioglioma), cavernoma, or focal cortical dysplasia; rule out alternative structural causes.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, prolactin (if drawn within 10–20 min of event), and AED levels if on therapy.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Exclude metabolic provocation (hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, uremia); baseline organ function for AED selection; AED level for adherence and dosing.

optimal_actions.action: Search current literature for AED selection in focal epilepsy and ILAE 2017 seizure classification.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Evidence-based AED options for focal epilepsy (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine, lacosamide); ILAE classification framework.

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions before initiating or modifying AED therapy (enzyme inducers, OCP, other CNS-active drugs).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Identify pharmacokinetic interactions (CYP induction by carbamazepine/phenytoin) and CNS adverse-effect overlap.

optimal_actions.action: Pursue prolonged video-EEG monitoring to capture habitual events, confirm lateralization, and evaluate surgical candidacy.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Capture of habitual focal seizure with electrographic correlate; concordance with imaging supports surgical workup.

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical features of CNS infection, encephalitis, or immunocompromise; CSF analysis is not indicated for routine focal epilepsy workup and exposes the patient to procedural risk and cost.
Episode semiology is clearly seizure-like; convulsive syncope is not on the differential, so ECG is low-yield.
No syncope-versus-seizure question and no structural-heart concern; echocardiogram contributes nothing to epilepsy workup.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is reserved for syncope-versus-seizure differentiation; not indicated when semiology is clearly epileptic.
Non-contrast head CT is inferior to MRI for detecting epileptogenic substrates (hippocampal sclerosis, FCD, low-grade tumor) and adds ionizing radiation without diagnostic yield.

sequence_constraints.reason: Structural cause influences AED choice (e.g., low-grade tumor → consider AEDs with CYP-neutral profile; hippocampal sclerosis → multiple equally appropriate options). MRI should inform drug selection.

critical_actions: Recognize olfactory hallucinations followed by behavioral arrest and oroalimentary automatisms as a mesial-temporal seizure semiology.
Pursue prolonged video-EEG monitoring when routine EEG is non-diagnostic to capture a habitual event.
Obtain dedicated 3T MRI epilepsy protocol to evaluate the hippocampi.
Initiate a first-line focal-epilepsy AED (e.g., lamotrigine, levetiracetam, lacosamide).
Counsel on driving restrictions and seizure safety, particularly with classroom occupation.
contraindicated_actions: Do not pursue ENT workup for the olfactory hallucinations in isolation — they are seizure aura.
Do not perform lumbar puncture without features of encephalitis.
Do not order a non-contrast head CT in lieu of MRI for epilepsy localization.
key_reasoning_points: Olfactory aura points to mesial-temporal origin (uncinate seizures).
Stereotyped behavioral arrest with oral automatisms and amnesia is the signature semiology of mesial TLE.
Routine EEG sensitivity is limited; prolonged video-EEG is the gold standard for capturing events and confirming lateralization.
3T MRI epilepsy protocol is needed to identify hippocampal sclerosis with confidence.
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: Laboratory testing does not diagnose focal epilepsy; it addresses a provoked seizure or a metabolic mimic when one is suspected.
